paras: The lynching of Granville Harrell was the hanging of a Black man by a mob near Raymond, Hinds County, Mississippi, on the night of December 18, 1880. Harrell was accused of killing his employer, David Simmons, a white Jackson meat-market keeper, with an ax two days earlier, and the sheriff had moved him to Raymond to keep him from a mob. A coroner's jury found that 75 to 100 unknown men had taken him from the jail and exonerated the officers. Mississippi papers reported the case within a week, and a short wire item carried it to papers from Louisiana to Wisconsin.

Harrell had long worked for Simmons, who kept a meat market in West Jackson. According to the Jackson Comet, there was "some trouble in regard to their financial affairs" between them, and they had been quarreling that morning. Other papers called the killing "unprovoked" or the result of "some imaginary offense."

According to the Jackson papers, on Thursday, December 16, Harrell struck Simmons with an ax when his back was turned and struck him again, crushing his skull; the Comet put the time at about 11 in the morning, a Picayune telegram at evening. Officer Fitzpatrick and others captured him, and the Comet wrote that a mob was gathering and the officer "barely succeeded" in getting him to jail. Harrell was reported to have confessed, and a coroner's jury found him "guilty of premeditated murder."

Fearing a lynching, Sheriff Morrison moved him that night from the Jackson jail to the one at Raymond. On Saturday night a body of men went to the Raymond jail, overpowered the jailer, took Harrell out and hanged him from a tree on the road outside town, near Snake Creek. A widely printed account said he clasped a post and that it took fifteen men to break his hold. The Clarion reported that he repeated his confession and implicated others, statements it declined to print.

The Raymond inquest, dated December 19, found that Harrell had been taken by "unknown men" and exonerated the sheriff and deputies, who had been compelled to give up the keys. He was buried Sunday morning by direction of the coroner. No report of arrests or prosecution of mob members appears in the coverage.

The Jackson weeklies treated the case mainly as the murder of a well-known citizen. The Clarion headlined "A CRUEL AND FOUL MURDER," called Harrell a "fiend" and gave most of its space to Simmons's life and funeral, describing the lynchers only as persons "whose names to this writer are unknown." The Comet headed its report "Swift Retribution" and printed only the inquest verdict. In another item it quoted the Raymond Gazette's history of the spot, where Black men had been lynched or shot by mobs in 1862, 1866 and 1875.

The Brookhaven Ledger began by saying that "Northern Republican papers are now furnished material for another Southern outrage" and described the mob as "whites and blacks." The Magnolia Gazette's short version named the dead man "J. B. Simmons" and placed the killing near Raymond. Outside Mississippi, papers from Louisiana to Wisconsin ran a one-line wire item that Harrel, "a negro," was lynched "by a masked party," or a longer "A Murderer Lynched" story that called Simmons "an old and respectable white man."

Estimates of the mob ranged from fifty masked men in the Picayune telegram to 75 to 100 at the inquest and 150 in the Brookhaven Ledger, which alone said it included Black men. The telegram put the hanging tree a short distance from the jail, while the inquest, a sworn local finding, placed the body outside the town limits.

bases: A mob took Harrell, accused of murder, from the Raymond jail and hanged him (A2, A7, A9).

Harrell was taken from jail by a mob of 50 to 150 men who overpowered the jailer and hanged him, without lawful authority, for the murder of David Simmons, which he was accused of and had confessed to (A2, A7, A9, A3).

Two Jackson weeklies, the Brookhaven Ledger, a Jackson telegram to the Picayune and the text of the Raymond inquest agree that a mob took Harrell from the Raymond jail and hanged him on the night of the 18th (A2, A3, A7, A9).

framing.detail: The Weekly Clarion headlined 'A Cruel and Foul Murder', called Harrell a 'fiend', eulogized Simmons, and reported the lynching briefly without comment, withholding Harrell's statements implicating others.
The Comet headed the lynching 'Swift Retribution' and said Harrell was 'unceremoniously taken' from jail, printing only the inquest verdict.
The Comet's first report praised the officer who saved Harrell from 'the enraged populace' while describing the 'old Satan in the negro'.
The Brookhaven Ledger opened by saying Northern Republican papers had material for 'another Southern outrage' and stressed that the mob included Black men.
Northern and Western papers ran a one-sentence brief that 'a negro' was 'lynched by a masked party', or the longer 'A Murderer Lynched' version.
